Activity 2: Your MGE

Your group will do a final project. Each person has a part to play. 

Your grade will be determined based upon the individual work you accomplished, but the more the group cooperates, the more likely you are to succeed.

Each group will have the following members. We used these same designations when I did my walkabouts of NJ, and they work really well for the division of labor.

Poison Ivy: Leader, will fill in jobs that are left undone, makes sure everyone knows what they are doing, and are on point.

Ant: Keeps track of meeting times, fills the sheets that outline who was present at each meeting and who did what for the final project.

Wolf: Makes sure that rules are respected, makes sure that there is no plagiarism, and that conflict is resolved in the group (some barking and some validating is required)

Bat: Is in charge of communication. Makes sure that everyone has each other’s contact information and establishes the best possible way for everyone to communicate.

Otter: Handles technical issues, in charge of editing, recording and film work. 

In charge doesn’t mean exclusive. Each task may require cooperation from various people. But the tasks determine whose academic “head will roll” if things aren’t done. The Poison Ivy’s head almost always rolls, but they aren’t the only one.

Here is your default issue. You can take on a different issue, if that's what your group decides, but remember that it has to be international and it has to require a measurable goal on both sides. Here are some possibilities:

Palestinians and Israelis setting parameters for safe May 15 protests.

Doctors without borders negotiate with EU officials to allow passage to a boatload of refugees from Lybia to Sicily.

Cattle ranchers vs. environmentalists or native peoples representatives in the Amazon

Inclusion of Taiwan in World Health Organization COVID coordination (one negotiator takes the side of China, the other of Taiwan)

Debate over shared power between Taliban forces and the government of Afghanistan

Nuclear Arms limitation in Iran (Iran and US negotiators)

  1. Choose an issue to work on
  2. Assign jobs and deadlines to accomplish those jobs
  3. Ant: Record who was present at this meeting, and in the last five minutes, ask each member of the cohort what they contributed to the project.
  4. Set up at least one time to meet outside of class time to work on the project, either on the dossier or on working on making the recording of the negotiation "work".
[googleapps domain="docs" dir="forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSe1ohEQPG4Z8vX2Oo9Si6rEVJHsLSC9YNXpVKGM1WAS_dxtqw/viewform" query="embedded=true" width="640" height="1073" /] [googleapps domain="docs" dir="document/d/e/2PACX-1vTNBXomEsh6m7mXmDGizy1X_Y7LVs3tCTtF6KGuv0zIcZne11aoGL0ZGAR99L3JMGyNy6OPHStfBSRO/pub" query="embedded=true" /]

As I reflect on the past semester, I have to say that this Intercultural Communication class, this particular collection of students was a silver lining in a crazy, often dark time. 

I admit that teaching you students, getting to know you as well as I could in this remote environment was often the highlight of my day.

So, thank you for getting up early, sharing your insights, letting me know what was going on with you. As long as Wordpress lasts, this class will be archived here, so if you want to leave a message to your future self, or students who will only experience what Covid was remotely, distantly, here’s a chance to leave something paraphrastic, or affective or dialectic on these pages. 

It may not be a huge legacy, but it’s something that some distant day, you may just revisit to amuse yourself. I leave the comment section open, and I ask you to leave a comment, maybe one thing you’ve learned from me, but even more importantly, something you’ve learned or benefitted from in your relationship with the other students in this class. Say something to your fellow classmates. 

There is an old story about an English Professor who, when giving the graduating class a speech, he said “I hope that after four years of study at this institution, you will have learned that it isn’t who you know, but whom you know.”

The point is, long after the main points of what is taught here have been rerouted through your dendrites and the neurons have stopped firing in that way that allows you to know concepts like grooming communities, Dunbar’s number, freeriders, empathy, uncertainty avoidance, cultural frameworks in general, TPAD’s and NSEW critiques, you will maintain some of the human connections you have made here. 


I will continue to hope to meet you in person in the fall, please, please come around. But even if I don’t see a single one of you, I do hope that at least some of you will see each other again,  maybe even for the first time.

Tying up loose ends, Part One.

14ymedio’s Faces of 2020: The Independent Artists of Cuba’s San Isidro Movement

14ymedio, Havana, 24 December 2020 – The San Isidro Movement, born just two years ago, has shaken the political situation in Cuba in the last weeks of 2020 by crossing borders and putting the regime in a bind of incalculable dimensions.

At the end of 2018, a group of independent artists who rejected Decree 349 – a law through which the Government sought to regulate the arts sector by making cultural work outside the state orbit de facto impossible – formed this movement in the Havana neighborhood that gave the movement its name.

The collective took center stage with a protest held in November to demand the release of one of its members, Denis Solís, sentenced to eight months in prison for the alleged crime of contempt. Several members of the group began a hunger and thirst strike, which some were able to maintain for more than a week until the headquarters of the Movement, where they were gathered, was raided by the political police, who detained them for several hours.

In solidarity with them, in addition to that they have found outside of Cuba, a group of at least 200 people demonstrated in Havana in an unusual protest that managed to begin a failed dialogue with the cultural authorities. The harassment of the Movement continues, with arrests, acts of repudiation and accusations of terrorism, but they have lit the fuse of a dream to open a new horizon for the opposition in 2021.

Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/him/his). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you are aware that culture itself evolves from the human instinct to both include and exclude others in order to acquire and distribute resources. This sounds cold, but resources can be wonderful intangibles, the seratonin release we feel, for instance is a resource, new, more efficient ways of doing things can also be a resource.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

I'm going to give away the entire plot right here at the beginning of the course: We humans have evolved a capacity to interact with a limited number of people (we will get to know Mr. Dunbar). The theorized upper level of people our brain has the capacity to know and have in our circles is 180 (with other theorists claiming that we can truly know up to 230 people).

We will study how a child learns culture and how that knowledge has an enormous impact on how that child remembers and sees the world. We will begin to understand the concept of schema, perception-action loop, habit and custom.

We will talk about the evolutionary reasons for cultural differentiation, and why we need language and culture to exclude "freeriders" from attempting to appropriate our resources, but we also need allies to help secure these resources.

While we may be excluded from a group, that should not surprise or offend us. We can actually admire and adapt aspects of other cultures that we are excluded from, and we can become "sojourners", people accepted as outsiders by other groups.

How will we use this information?

We will also study and attempt to develop ways to move from the status of outsider to insider quickly while reducing cultural shock. This ability to move has deep implications for people who study marketing and publicity, peacemaking, art, religion and even health studies.

We will study intercultural win-win negotiation, and hopefully give you some tools you can use in your everyday life to move towards agreement and consensus.

We will use our knowledge to begin to understand the way resource distribution, and therefore culture itself, is driven and changed by what I call "engines of cultural change". These are: economics, technology, disaster, belief, family, religion, geography, ideas, education and individuals. We will examine how these engines interact to create and sustain culture.

Along the way, you will:

  1. Learn to write a T-PAD
  2. Study your own heritage
  3. Learn about New Jersey and share your knowledge with the world (creating a display for the Peace Corps display case in The Great Hall, and sending those very NJ items to children somewhere in the world)
  4. Learn about cultural taxonomy and frameworks and how they explain our actions.
  5. Work as a team to create a cultural consulting group that advises an individual on a real-life cultural problem.

I love teaching this course. It's one of my all-time favorites to teach. I hope that this format will be useful to you and that you will surprise yourself with what you accomplish and how it can help you out there in the world.

So let's get started with our goals for today. In today's class, we will get to know each other a little better, we will learn the routine of the class, we will discover what a T-PAD is, and we will cover the syllabus.

Why WordPress?

I chose to use WordPress as our default platform because I believe that it is important that you create work that you can share with future classes and to create a work that you can share with the world. When you spend a great deal of time writing a paper, generally the only people to ever read that paper are you and your professor. I think that definitely influences what you believe and hope in terms of the quality of your work. I teach this course almost every semester, and I hope that by using WordPress, I'm creating a "dynamic textbook" which will allow your contribution to be shared forever. I'm hoping you will create work that should be shared forever.

That being said, you might sometimes want to create a redacted version of your work for public viewing. The way to do that is to create your text, submit it on ecampus as usual, and then delete the information you do not wish to share. Then paste what's left to WordPress.

I also use WordPress because it allows me to embed elements of the entire class in a single webpage. You will see google docs and google forms, for instance, which you can access directly on this site. I hope that doing so will help make this semester easier to navigate.

What will happen each class?

I understand zoom burnout, and don't want you to suffer. I divide my class into five sections when I teach live, and for ten minutes or so, the cohorts (groups of five) rotate through five tasks. I will be assigning permanent cohorts by class. This means you MUST sign in through monmouth.zoom.us . It is an essential time saver and we will go over how to do that.

Each Monday you will get a short reading that you can probably do in class, but to hand in no later than 4:30 on Tuesday if you want to be graded out of 100 and each Wednesday you will get a longer reading that you will have to turn in by Friday by 4:30 if you want to be graded out of 100. My goal this semester is to attempt to have neither of us work on weekends, and I will be grading your work at 4:30 on Tuesdays and Fridays. Please let me know if the work I assign is too much.

  3. How often do you eat with your hands versus with a utensil per week? How often is meat part of your meal? Fish?
  4. Do you eat facing each other, or a screen? How far in advance is a meal planned?
  5. How often is the meal in your home cooked versus purchased?
  6. What are the major eating holidays?

Activity 4:

In the previous round, you did a survey that talked about Geert Hofsteade's cultural dimensions test and you took a survey that compared your own dimensions to that of a specific country. Now, as a group, look at the cultural dimensions we measured. Talk about your own upbringing and your local culture. Read the dimensions and describe where you as an individual, as a member of your family and larger community fit within these dynamics. Often in cultures of immigrants, there is a disconnect between the cultural dynamic in the household and the one "on the street".

High vs. Low Power Distance: Refers to the beliefs regarding the proper distribution of power in a society. It expresses how much less powerful members of a community should accept that power is allocated unequally. How a society deals with social inequality is the main concern in this dimension. People in civilizations with high power distance accept hierarchical structures where everyone has a place, and no further reasoning is necessary to justify that hierarchy. In comparison, societies with low levels of power distance work to equalize power distribution and demand tangible reasons for power inequalities in the government of their countries. Do older siblings get privileges that younger ones don't? Do bosses get privileges that workers don't?

Individualism vs. Collectivism: Indicates how the interests of the individual are weighed against the interest of the community. A loosely-knit social structure in which people are expected to look out for and check in primarily with themselves denotes a high level of individualism. By contrast, cultures with low levels of individualism are attuned toward the group and typically feature a closely-knit social structure in which people look to their relatives, countrymen, coworkers, and other members of their communities when determining what course of action they will take. Does the good of the many outweigh the good of the one? Should you go as far as your abilities will allow? Should it be "from each, according to his ability, to each according to his need?"

Masculinity vs. Femininity: Cultures high in masculinity tend to revolve around success, competition, and rewards. By contrast, cultures low in masculinity concentrate on values like nurture, modesty, and empathy. High-masculinity cultures often produce more assertive and decisive leaders, whereas low-masculinity cultures tend to produce more agreeable, inclusive, and compassionate leaders. Is this a problematic way to see masculinity and femininity?

High vs. Low Uncertainty Avoidance: Measures how comfortable a culture is with ambiguity and uncertainty. High uncertainty avoidance cultures uphold strict moral and behavioral standards and tend to frown on unconventional behavior and ideas. They want the future taken care of and planned for according to what has been proven to work in the past. By contrast, low uncertainty avoidance cultures are more tolerant of unusual ways of doing things and are not as disapproving of ambiguity.

Long vs. Short-term Orientation: Measures whether a culture aims for long-term goals on the basis of how the world is projected to change or prefers to achieve short-term goals using how things have been up till now as a guide. Cultures with a long-term orientation are future-focused and promote thrift and investments that take a long time to come to fruition. In contrast, cultures with short-term orientation uphold long-standing traditions as a way of ensuring stability and tempering the speed of social change. I put a syllabus together with a timetable, but that has changed, and it may not be clear to people. What does that indicate about the culture of this class? How could that cause culture shock?

Indulgence vs. Restraint: Measures the degree to which cultures attempt to regulate their impulses toward gratification. Cultures high in indulgence encourage pleasure and enjoyment as innate human desires associated with taking pleasure in life and having fun, whereas cultures with a restraint orientation frown on the satisfaction of desires and attempt to control enjoyment through social rules and taboos. Where do your people fit in? Are you an athlete? Do you think this standard is different among athletes?

  1. Individualism vs. Collectivism:
    • Did you attend schools where teamwork and group projects were emphasized, or were you primarily assessed based on individual performance?

Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/él). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you have a good technique for negotiating, and you understand that the real purpose of (intercultural) negotiating is to establish a relationship from which you can build solutions, not necessarily for coming up with solutions immediately.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

Why is this critical, especially in this class?

Because if you can't get along with your own cohort, that may be from a similar cultural background, what possible chance do you have to get along with people who have vastly different backgrounds?

Along the way, you will:

  1. Learn to write a T-PAD
  2. Learn how to negotiate across culture
  3. Learn about New Jersey and share your knowledge with the world (
  4. Learn about cultural taxonomy (cultural dimensions) and frameworks and how they explain our actions.

I love teaching this course. It's one of my all-time favorites to teach. I hope that this format will be useful to you and that you will surprise yourself with what you accomplish and how it can help you out there in the world.

So let's get started with our goals for today. In today's class, we will get to know each other a little better, we will learn the routine of the class, we will discover what a T-PAD is, and we will cover the syllabus.

Why WordPress?

I chose to use WordPress as our default platform because I believe that it is important that you create work that you can share with future classes and to create a work that you can share with the world. When you spend a great deal of time writing a paper, generally the only people to ever read that paper are you and your professor. I think that definitely influences what you believe and hope in terms of the quality of your work. I teach this course almost every semester, and I hope that by using WordPress, I'm creating a "dynamic textbook" which will allow your contribution to be shared forever. I'm hoping you will create work that should be shared forever.

That being said, you might sometimes want to create a redacted version of your work for public viewing. The way to do that is to create your text, submit it on ecampus as usual, and then delete the information you do not wish to share. Then paste what's left to WordPress.

I also use WordPress because it allows me to embed elements of the entire class in a single webpage. You will see google docs and google forms, for instance, which you can access directly on this site. I hope that doing so will help make this semester easier to navigate.

What will happen each class?

We will have a walk on song, a short lecture and rotate through stations that reinforce the work we do in our class.

Please understand that I myself am part of an older tradition that emphasized student input, discovery and error as part of a process. Students who are used to looking for clear expectations, who feel that they can stay ahead of the curve by doing assignments written into a calendar, and basically checking boxes, might feel discouraged by this class. If you want to go ahead, explore other areas of inquiry, do other readings, use this class to answer questions I haven't asked, just let me know and we can work out a way for this to happen, as long as your avenues of inquiry pull the class along with you.

What this means is that you will not see a class that shows slides, assigns readings, tells you what is on a test and then you study, learn what the test entails, and then do some presentations or papers that further illustrate the points made.

We live in exciting times, and I am excited to see what use you make of new tools emerging. I am hoping that in short order, you will be able to take over the class and teach me something. If all you get out of the class is a good grade, then you may have passed the class, but the class has failed you.

    Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/él). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

    If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you are aware that culture itself evolves from the human instinct to both include and exclude others in order to acquire and distribute resources. This sounds cold, but resources can be wonderful intangibles, the seratonin release we feel, for instance is a resource, new, more efficient ways of doing things can also be a resource.

    If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

    I'm going to give away the entire plot right here at the beginning of the course: We humans may or may not have evolved a capacity to interact with a limited number of people (we will get to know Mr. Dunbar). The theorized upper level of people our brain has the capacity to know and have in our circles is 180 (with other theorists claiming that we can truly know up to 230 people).

    We will study how a child learns culture and how that knowledge has an enormous impact on how that child remembers and sees the world. We will begin to understand the concept of schema, perception-action loop, habit and custom.

    We will talk about the evolutionary reasons for cultural differentiation, and why we need language and culture to exclude "freeriders" from attempting to appropriate our resources, but we also need allies to help secure these resources.

    While we may be excluded from a group, that should not surprise or offend us. We can actually admire and adapt aspects of other cultures that we are excluded from, and we can become "sojourners", people accepted as outsiders by other groups.

    How will we use this information?

    We will also study and attempt to develop ways to move from the status of outsider to insider quickly while reducing cultural shock. This ability to move has deep implications for people who study marketing and publicity, peacemaking, art, religion and even health studies.

    We will study intercultural win-win negotiation, and hopefully give you some tools you can use in your everyday life to move towards agreement and consensus.

    We will use our knowledge to begin to understand the way resource distribution, and therefore culture itself, is driven and changed by what I call "engines of cultural change". These are: economics, technology, disaster, belief, family, religion, geography, ideas, education and individuals. We will examine how these engines interact to create and sustain culture.

    Along the way, you will:

    1. Learn to write a T-PAD

    I love teaching this course. It's one of my all-time favorites to teach. I hope that this format will be useful to you and that you will surprise yourself with what you accomplish and how it can help you out there in the world.

    So let's get started with our goals for today. In today's class, we will get to know each other a little better, we will learn the routine of the class, we will discover what a T-PAD is, and we will cover the syllabus.

[googlemaps https://www.google.com/maps/d/embed?mid=1FwpznZKpgTr66BNRuvkSf9FCZF83NIBF&w=640&h=480]

Individualism: A belief system that prioritizes personal independence, self-reliance, and individual goals over the needs of the group.

Collectivism: A worldview that emphasizes group cohesion, shared responsibilities, and placing the group’s interests above individual desires.

High-context Culture: A setting where much of the information is implied or understood through background knowledge, with a focus on non-verbal cues and shared assumptions.

Low-context Culture: A setting where information is conveyed explicitly, with clear, direct verbal expression and less reliance on shared assumptions or non-verbal hints.

Power Distance: The degree to which a society accepts and expects an unequal distribution of authority and status within its institutions.

Uncertainty Avoidance: The extent to which a society feels threatened by ambiguity or change, leading to a preference for clear rules and predictable outcomes.

Time Orientation: The perspective a culture holds regarding the past, present, or future, influencing how time is valued and managed.

Masculinity: A societal preference for traits like competitiveness, assertiveness, and the pursuit of material success.

Femininity: A societal preference for traits such as nurturing, cooperation, and a focus on caring for others.

Long-term Orientation: A worldview that emphasizes perseverance, thrift, and planning for future outcomes over short-term gains.

Short-term Orientation: A focus on achieving quick results and maintaining respect for traditions rather than planning far into the future.

Nature Relatedness: The way a society interacts with the natural environment, ranging from attempts to control or exploit it to living in balance with it.

Formality: A cultural emphasis on strict social norms, protocols, and adherence to hierarchies, including the use of titles and proper etiquette.

Informality: A cultural tendency toward relaxed social norms, flexible interactions, and downplaying hierarchical structures.

Monochronic Time: A cultural approach to time that views it as linear and compartmentalized, focusing on doing one task at a time and following strict schedules.

Polychronic Time: A cultural approach that views time as fluid, allowing for multitasking and flexible scheduling.

Face-saving: The practice of preserving one’s dignity or avoiding embarrassment in social situations, often by being careful about how one’s actions are perceived.

Gender Roles: The societal expectations regarding the behaviors and responsibilities assigned to men and women.

Cultural Conformity: A tendency to adhere to shared norms, practices, and traditions, often discouraging deviation from accepted social behaviors.

What does the 7-38-55% rule have to do with negotiation?

  • Observe your counterpart’s body language. According to the 7-38-55 rule, 93 percent of meaning is communicated non-verbally. Your tone of voice and body language are much more important than what you’re actually saying. If your counterpart’s body language indicates that they are about to lose their bearings, speak calmly and plainly to soothe them and slow the pace of the negotiation. You should always seek a course of action that encourages the other side to let their guard down. In an effective negotiation, you should try to build a working relationship with your negotiating partner and find ways to defuse tension when possible.
  • Look for inconsistencies between spoken words and nonverbal behavior. When you’re at the negotiating table, pay attention to how your counterparts speak and act. Do the words they’re saying match the way they’re carrying themselves? Look at the people who are not talking—what does their body language signal to you? Remember that their spoken words only account for seven percent of their communication and look for nonverbal cues that contradict their words. It’s also important that you make sure your own nonverbal messages are in line with what you are saying. If your facial expressions are pained and you can’t maintain eye contact, you are communicating your insecurity to your counterpart no matter what you say.
  • Monitor your counterpart’s speaking patterns. We all have one way of telling the truth. If you can identify how your counterpart looks and sounds when they are being honest with you, you’ll be able to detect any deviations from that pattern that may signal a lie. People who are being dishonest tend to use more words and effort than necessary to communicate their point. Use your listening skills to keep an ear out for such verbosity and gain an upper hand.
  • Learn to use different vocal tones. According to the 7-38-55 rule, tone of voice accounts for 38 percent of meaning in communication. Mastering the use of your voice can help you become a better negotiator by improving the delivery of your arguments. In the negotiating room, there are three main tones of voice: Assertive voice is declarative and typically counterproductive. An accommodating voice gently promotes collaboration and should be used most of the time.
  • Calibrate your own nonverbal communication. Effective communication during a negotiation, conflict management session, or problem-solving sessions requires the ability to calibrate how you communicate. Tap into your listening skills, assess how your counterpart is feeling, and adjust your nonverbal communication in response. This will communicate far more about your reaction than anything you could say to them. When debating the main points in a negotiation, try to alter your demeanor based on the signals you are receiving from your counterpart. Even if your arguments themselves don’t change, changing your nonverbal messaging can be effective.

Workshop with tone of voice and nonverbal communication.

Active listening... be curious about the person, quiet the voices in your own head.

Use the "calibrated no"

1. “Is now a bad time to talk?”

Replaces: 

  • “Have you got a few minutes to talk?” 
  • “Is now a good time to talk?”

Why use this:

  • This is a great way to practice getting your repetitions in with no-oriented questions and seeing their effectiveness in action.
  • People feel anxious when they sense you are seeking a yes. This relieves your counterpart from wondering what they are getting themselves into if they agree.
  • People feel safe and secure when they say no. This is a great way to learn this concept.

You will only ever get two answers to this question:

  • “Not at all! It’s never a bad time to talk to you. What have you got?” Or something very close to this. When you get a response like this you now have their complete attention—which is what you were after in the first place.)
  • “Yes, it is a bad time. But I can talk with you at (a time they suggest).” Perfect. Again, this is what you were after—their focused attention.

I’m sure you’re wondering: What if they say yes and don’t give you a good time to talk? 

Consider this: Do you want to be on the phone with someone who responds like that? Someone else out there is waiting for you, and this call is keeping you from them. Move on. 

Stop making compromises.  Download our guide to negotiating contracts and learn how to never settle »

2. “Is it a ridiculous idea … ?”

Replaces:    

  • “Is this a good idea?” 
  • “Would you like to do this?”
  • “Does this look like something that would work for you?”
  • “Would you be willing to … ?”

Why use this: 

  • See above re: No. 1. 

This replaces the clarification and micro-commitments of yes-oriented questions.

Also realize that you will often get “No, but …” as a response. The information you get after the “but” is exactly what you need to understand the obstacles standing between you and implementation. This is crucial for solving those obstacles—if they can be solved. If not, you can move on with a clear conscience. 

3. “Are you against … ?”

Replaces: 

  • “Do you agree?” (“Do you disagree?” is also acceptable here as a replacement.)
  • “Will you … ?”
  • “Are you in favor of … ?”
  • “Does this look like something that will work for you?”

Why use this:

It replaces the commitment of yes-oriented questions. This is very similar to the second no-oriented question on this list. Both can also be used in combination for clarification of details and commitment to action.   

4. “Have you given up on … ?”

Replaces:   

  • “Do you still want … ?”
  • “Are you still interested in … ?”
  • Any communication to check in with someone who has stopped communicating with you.

This is also the best way to restart communication!

We are going to look at Agents of Change. Two major agents of change are technology and crisis. After this video was made, post-covid PISA scores began to plummet in Finland. The cultural freedom that children had to be children meant an early adoption of devices without limitation. Finland now ranks 11th among nations for reading and math. Globally, reading scores declined by fifteen points and math scores by twenty points. The Pandemic accounts for some of this, but the scores had been declining before the Pandemic. China severely limits and controls use of cellphones among children under the age of 18.

  • Children under 8 are limited to 40 minutes of phone use per day.
  • Those aged 8-16 are allowed 1 hour of screen time daily
  • No one under 18 can to access their screens between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. while using the minor mode.
  1. Additional features:
  • The minor mode automatically closes online applications when time limits are reached.
  • Users receive a reminder to rest after using their device for more than 30 minutes.
Declining PISA Scores Finland, once renowned for its high-achieving students, has experienced a steady decline in its PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment) scores since 2007, coinciding with the introduction of smartphones1. The latest PISA study revealed Finland's lowest-ever average scores in math, science, and reading, prompting the Finnish Ministry of Education and Culture to describe the situation as "extremely disconcerting"1. Digital Distraction The 2022 PISA data showed that over 80% of Finland's 15-year-olds reported being distracted by digital devices during math class, at least sometimes1. This high level of distraction is strongly associated with lower academic achievement. Excessive Screen Time Finnish teenagers reported spending more than four hours on digital devices during the school day, ranking Finland sixth overall in digital device usage at school according to the 2022 PISA study1. This excessive screen time is likely contributing to the erosion of learning outcomes. Early Smartphone Adoption A particularly concerning trend in Finland is the early age at which children receive smartphones: Most Finnish children receive their first smartphone (or smartwatch) at age 5 or 61. A 2022 survey indicated that virtually all first-graders in Finland owned phones, including phone watches1. This early adoption of smartphones may be exacerbating the "phone-based childhood" phenomenon, which has been linked to sleep loss, addiction, attention problems, and social deprivation1.

pages.full_content:
You can locate yourself in the classroom, but we are not going to finish the video in class, so you also have to locate yourself somewhere else.

Think about the filmmaker's relationship to time. Think about the cultural dimensions from the filmmaker's point of view.

Things to look for:

How do we do that?

Time orientation

1. Individualism vs. Collectivism

What to Look For:

  • Are success and fulfillment tied to individual pursuits or collective well-being?
  • Does the filmmaker celebrate or critique characters for breaking away from or adhering to societal norms?

Examples:

  1. Collectivism (Family and Community Focused):
    • Film: "Encanto" (2021)
      • Focus: Family sacrifice and harmony.
      • The Madrigal family’s collective efforts define their success, though the protagonist challenges unbalanced expectations within the family.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker portrays success as maintaining family bonds while recognizing individual contributions, emphasizing collectivist values.
  2. Individualism (Personal Freedom and Independence):
    • Film: "Everything Everywhere All at Once" (2022)
      • Focus: The protagonist, Evelyn, explores infinite possibilities to find personal fulfillment while navigating family relationships.
      • Analysis: Individual self-discovery is key to the film’s resolution, though it balances this with reconciling familial love, reflecting a nuanced take on individualism.

2. Power Distance

What to Look For:

  • Are characters rewarded for challenging authority, or for adhering to hierarchical structures?
  • Does the filmmaker critique or support traditional power dynamics?

Examples:

  1. High Power Distance (Respecting Authority):
    • Film: "The Woman King" (2022)
      • Focus: Leadership and loyalty within a hierarchical kingdom.
      • Characters thrive by respecting their roles within the societal structure, while power dynamics are acknowledged as central to their survival.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker highlights the benefits of loyalty and leadership within a power structure, affirming high power distance.
  2. Low Power Distance (Challenging Authority):
    • Film: "Black Panther" (2018)
      • Focus: Questioning traditional authority for progressive change.
      • T’Challa faces challenges to the throne, with success ultimately framed as evolving the monarchy to embrace new values.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker critiques rigid hierarchies while offering a vision for leadership rooted in equity and questioning tradition.

3. Masculinity vs. Femininity

What to Look For:

  • Does success depend on competition and dominance (masculinity) or cooperation and emotional fulfillment (femininity)?
  • Are traditional gender roles reinforced, challenged, or subverted?

Examples:

  1. Masculinity (Achievement and Competition):
    • Film: "Top Gun: Maverick" (2022)
      • Focus: Competition, heroism, and ambition.
      • Success is framed as achieving excellence and leadership through intense competition and skill.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker reinforces traditional masculine ideals, celebrating achievement and personal valor.
  2. Femininity (Cooperation and Relationships):
    • Film: "Barbie" (2023)
      • Focus: Self-discovery and societal transformation.
      • The narrative emphasizes emotional fulfillment, cooperation, and redefining one’s identity beyond societal expectations.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker critiques rigid roles while celebrating emotional intelligence and collective growth.

4. High Context vs. Low Context Communication

What to Look For:

  • Does the film emphasize subtle, indirect communication (high context) or explicit, direct dialogue (low context)?
  • Are non-verbal cues or visual symbolism central to the storytelling?

Examples:

  1. High Context (Subtle Communication):
    • Film: "Drive My Car" (2021)
      • Focus: Silence, subtext, and emotional complexity.
      • The story unfolds through subtle interactions, leaving much to interpretation through visual and emotional cues.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker demonstrates the richness of indirect communication, reflecting high-context storytelling.
  2. Low Context (Direct Communication):
    • Film: "Marriage Story" (2019)
      • Focus: Explicit, raw dialogue in conflict.
      • Success or resolution comes through direct conversations about the characters’ struggles and emotions.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker emphasizes low-context communication, where words explicitly drive the narrative and resolution.

5. Uncertainty Avoidance

What to Look For:

  • Does the film celebrate taking risks, or does success come from adhering to stability and tradition?
  • Are characters rewarded or punished for embracing ambiguity?

Examples:

  1. High Uncertainty Avoidance (Stability and Structure):
    • Film: "The Banshees of Inisherin" (2022)
      • Focus: Avoiding change and preserving tradition.
      • Characters struggle to reconcile their need for stability with the disruption of personal relationships.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker explores the cost of breaking stability, aligning with high uncertainty avoidance.
  2. Low Uncertainty Avoidance (Risk and Ambiguity):
    • Film: "Dune" (2021)
      • Focus: Embracing risk to fulfill a destiny.
      • Success lies in navigating uncertainty and accepting the ambiguity of the protagonist’s future.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker celebrates risk-taking and adaptability, aligning with low uncertainty avoidance.

6. Time Orientation (Long-Term vs. Short-Term)

What to Look For:

  • Are characters motivated by tradition and legacy (long-term orientation) or immediate goals and gratification (short-term orientation)?
  • How does the film frame success: as enduring and gradual or as immediate and fleeting?
  • Does the filmmaker expect the audience to be patient as the story unfolds?

Examples:

  1. Long-Term Orientation (Legacy and Patience):
    • Film: "Oppenheimer" (2023)
      • Focus: The long-term consequences of innovation and legacy.
      • Success is framed as bittersweet, with the character grappling with the lasting impact of his scientific contributions.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker emphasizes legacy and the moral weight of decisions over time.
  2. Short-Term Orientation (Immediate Gratification):
    • Film: "Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery" (2022)
      • Focus: The pursuit of short-term personal gains and immediate resolution.
      • Success is achieved through clever, short-term problem-solving and exposing deception.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker critiques short-term thinking while entertaining its immediate appeal.
  3. Long Term Orientation for the filmmaker
    • Roma
      • Focus: frame shots do not change quickly
      • The film lingers over scenes

7. Relationship with Nature

What to Look For:

  • Is nature portrayed as something to be controlled (mastery) or something to coexist with (harmony)?
  • How does the filmmaker frame success in relation to the environment?

Examples:

7. Relationship with Nature (Expanded)

What to Look For:

  • Cinematography and Framing:
    • Are characters shown as dominating the environment (foregrounded, large in the frame)?
    • Or are they integrated into the landscape (smaller, more balanced with the natural surroundings)?
    • Does the filmmaker emphasize the environment as a passive backdrop or an active, living entity?
  • Symbolism of Nature:
    • Is nature depicted as something to be controlled and overcome, or something to live in harmony with?
    • Does the film celebrate the beauty of the natural world, or does it use the environment to highlight human power, struggle, or isolation?

Examples:

  1. Mastery Over Nature (Foregrounding Characters):
    • Film: "The Martian" (2015)
      • Cinematography: The protagonist (Matt Damon) is foregrounded against the stark, barren Martian landscape, emphasizing human resilience and ingenuity in mastering a hostile environment.
      • Focus: Survival is achieved by reshaping and controlling nature through science and determination.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker frames success as humanity’s ability to overcome natural obstacles, aligning with a mastery-over-nature perspective.
  2. Harmony with Nature (Foregrounding Environment):
    • Film: "Nomadland" (2020)
      • Cinematography: The vast landscapes often dwarf the protagonist, highlighting her small, yet deeply connected place in the natural world. The environment is as much a character as the humans.
      • Focus: The protagonist finds peace and purpose by moving through natural spaces, embracing harmony with the environment.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker portrays success as accepting and finding one’s place within the natural world, reflecting a coexistence mindset.
  3. Duality of Nature (Shifting Focus):
    • Film: "The Revenant" (2015)
      • Cinematography: Characters are sometimes foregrounded in extreme close-ups, showing their struggle against nature, but the camera frequently pulls back to immerse viewers in the majesty and hostility of the environment.
      • Focus: The film depicts nature as both a source of danger and beauty, testing humanity’s resilience while respecting its power.
      • Analysis: The filmmaker emphasizes the duality of nature, where success comes from endurance and adaptation rather than domination.

How Framing Reflects Success

  1. Foregrounding People:
  2. The Bear (TV)
    • Cinematography: Human close-ups, tight angles, almost always in a home or at the restaurant, not much engagement with nature at all.
    • Analysis: The very absence of nature and the focus on the human shows that the filmmaker does not focus on the natural world.
  3. Foregrounding Nature:
    • Suggests coexistence or insignificance of humanity compared to the vastness of nature.
    • Example: In "My Octopus Teacher" (2020), the underwater world overshadows the protagonist, emphasizing harmony, respect, and learning from nature.
  4. Shared Space (Balanced Framing):
    • Suggests interdependence between humans and nature.
    • Example: In "Moana" (2016), the ocean and environment are central, often sharing equal framing with the protagonist, symbolizing mutual respect and partnership.

Questions:

  • How does the filmmaker use framing to position characters in relation to their environment?
  • Are characters depicted as more significant than their surroundings, or as part of the natural world?
  • What do these visual choices say about the cultural attitude toward nature (mastery, harmony, or interdependence)?
  • Does the film’s resolution reflect success as conquering nature, surviving it, or living in harmony with it?

You final.

We are going to talk about the final today.

You are going to be assigned a country and a negotiation goal.

First, you have to validate a concern. You have been sent to one of these countries to determine what the concern, or issue is, surrounding what is going on. Use validation techniques, but sensitive to the cultural dimensions to establish what your counterpart wants.

Your job:

  1. Representing one of the players, your first job is to validate the claim of the person you are negotiating with. You need to do that within the context of the culture you are addressing. Use the validation script, but modify it to account for cultural differences.

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Kurdish Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Strong collective identity
  • Family/tribal honor central
  • Shared historical context
  • Community-based understanding

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with appropriate Kurdish greetings and honorifics: "Roj baş" (Good day) with proper respect markers

Listen while:

  • Showing deep respect for tribal/family status
  • Maintaining appropriate eye contact
  • Acknowledging group presence if applicable
  • Showing patience with narrative

2. Reflection Phase

"With respect to you and your family..." "If I understand our discussion..."

Mirror while:

  • Including collective context
  • Acknowledging family honor
  • Respecting tribal traditions
  • Maintaining appropriate formality

3. Verification Phase

"Have I honored your meaning correctly?" "Please guide me if I have misunderstood..."

4. Continuation Phase

"Our people have much wisdom to share..." "Please continue if there is more to tell..."

5. Validation Phase

"This understanding comes from our shared experiences..." "One can see how our people's wisdom shows..."

6. Empathy Phase

Collective emphasis: "Our community carries such experiences..." "Many among us would feel deeply about..."

7. Closing Phase

"Thank you for sharing this wisdom..." "May our people continue to support each other..."

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Honor tribal/family connections
  • Acknowledge collective struggles
  • Respect traditional hierarchies
  • Include community context
  • Reference shared cultural understanding

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Russian Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Formal but direct communication
  • Strong respect for hierarchy
  • Less emphasis on positive reframing
  • Professional distance maintained

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin formally using proper name and patronymic: "[Name] [Patronymic], I am ready to listen."

Listen while:

  • Maintaining professional posture
  • Showing attention through direct eye contact
  • Limiting verbal interruptions
  • Respecting hierarchy

2. Reflection Phase

Direct but formal: "If I understand correctly, [Name] [Patronymic]..." "Allow me to reflect what you have shared..."

Mirror while:

  • Maintaining formal language
  • Being direct but respectful
  • Acknowledging position/status
  • Keeping professional distance

3. Verification Phase

Clear but formal checking: "Have I understood your position correctly?" "Please correct any misunderstanding."

4. Continuation Phase

"Would you like to add anything further?" "Please continue if there are additional points."

5. Validation Phase

Direct but respectful: "Your position is logical considering..." "One can understand your conclusion based on..."

6. Empathy Phase

Reserved but acknowledging: "Such a situation would naturally be challenging..." "One can understand the seriousness of this position..."

7. Closing Phase

Professional closing: "Thank you for sharing your perspective." "Your input is valued and understood."

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Maintain professional boundaries
  • Respect hierarchical structures
  • Limit excessive emotional expression
  • Focus on practical understanding
  • Acknowledge position/status

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Iranian Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Incorporate ta'arof (ritual courtesy)
  • Poetic/indirect communication
  • High context culture
  • Strong emphasis on social harmony

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with formal greetings: "Salaam" (with appropriate honorifics - "Agha" for men, "Khanoom" for women)

Listen while:

  • Showing deference through body language
  • Using appropriate verbal acknowledgments
  • Maintaining respectful eye contact
  • Practicing patience with narrative style

2. Reflection Phase

With extreme courtesy: "If I may be so honored to reflect your precious words..." "With your gracious permission, I understood that..."

Mirror while:

  • Using poetic language when appropriate
  • Maintaining formal address
  • Including social context
  • Acknowledging family honor

3. Verification Phase

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with appropriate greeting: "Merhaba" (or "Selamün aleyküm" if appropriate) Express honor at listening: "It would be my honor to listen to your thoughts on this matter."

Listen attentively while:

2. Reflection Phase

When the speaker pauses, respond: "Sayın [appropriate title], if I may reflect what you have shared..." [using formal language] OR "[Title] Bey/Hanım, with your permission, I understand that..." [for less formal situations]

Mirror content while:

  • Maintaining formal language

3. Verification Phase

  • Increase indirect communication with higher status individuals

Negotiation Scenarios Chart for Key players in Syria

Here are the key interests of all players, besides the US and Israel.

First, express a concern across culture. For instance, you are a sojourner into Iranian culture. Use this chart to help, and then each of you conduct a Black Swan-type negotiation.

Now, Russia wants guarantees of safety to their personnel and equipment evacuating Syria.

Key Observations

  1. Competing Interests:
    • Most players (Turkey, Kurds, Syria) have overlapping but conflicting territorial and sovereignty goals, especially in northern Syria.
    • Iran and Russia align in supporting Assad but differ on their ultimate long-term influence.
  2. Potential Areas of Agreement:
    • Stabilization of Syria is a shared goal for all parties, though the definition of "stabilization" varies.
    • Economic incentives (e.g., reconstruction contracts) could be used as leverage for cooperation.
  3. Points of Leverage:
    • Turkey can leverage its control of border zones and refugee management.
    • Russia has influence over both the Syrian government and Turkey.
    • The Kurds have strategic importance as a buffer against extremists and Turkish incursions.

Here are obstacles to asks and offers:

Turkey

  • Obstacle 1: Limiting Pressure on Iranian-Backed Militias
    • Issue: Turkey risks straining its relations with the U.S., which opposes Iranian influence in Syria.
    • Impact: This could jeopardize U.S. military and economic support, including arms deals and NATO coordination.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey might seek to reassure the U.S. by emphasizing its role in countering Russian influence or combatting ISIS.
  • Obstacle 2: Collaboration with Russia
    • Issue: Turkey’s cooperation with Russia, such as on the TurkStream pipeline and northern Syria zones, often conflicts with U.S. and NATO interests.
    • Impact: Strains NATO unity and risks sanctions, such as those imposed after Turkey purchased the Russian S-400 missile system.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey uses its control over NATO’s southern flank and refugee management as leverage.
  • Obstacle 3: Continued Incursions into Kurdish Areas
    • Issue: Aggressive actions against Kurdish forces may alienate both the U.S. (which supports the Syrian Democratic Forces, or SDF) and Russia (which prefers regional stability).
    • Impact: This could result in diminished influence in broader negotiations or loss of Kurdish cooperation in countering extremism.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey could offer limited recognition of Kurdish cultural rights to de-escalate tensions.

Iran

  • Obstacle 1: Supporting Syrian Government
    • Issue: Iran’s backing of Assad and militias alienates the U.S., Israel, and Turkey, and makes broader regional cooperation difficult.
    • Impact: Increases economic sanctions and diplomatic isolation.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could propose scaling back its forces in exchange for reduced U.S. pressure or security guarantees from Israel.
  • Obstacle 2: Conflict with Turkey
    • Issue: Iranian-backed militias operate near Turkish zones of influence, creating direct tensions.
    • Impact: Hinders Iranian-Turkish collaboration on broader regional issues.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could focus on mediating Kurdish-Turkish tensions to find common ground.
  • Obstacle 3: Expanding Influence
    • Issue: Iran’s growing influence in Syria is a direct threat to Israel, leading to frequent Israeli airstrikes and opposition from Gulf states.
    • Impact: Escalates military risks and complicates relations with Russia, which seeks stability in Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could negotiate with Russia to limit its visibility near Israeli borders.

Syrian Government

  • Obstacle 1: Reconciling with Kurds
    • Issue: Offering autonomy to the Kurds could alienate Turkey, which opposes any Kurdish self-governance.
    • Impact: Risks Turkish retaliation or increased military presence in northern Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could frame Kurdish autonomy as limited to cultural or administrative matters.
  • Obstacle 2: Dependence on Iran and Russia
    • Issue: Heavy reliance on Iranian and Russian support limits Assad’s flexibility in negotiations with Turkey, Kurds, and Western powers.
    • Impact: Creates a perception of diminished sovereignty and weakens bargaining power.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could seek balanced deals that allow limited concessions to Western interests while maintaining Russian and Iranian support.
  • Obstacle 3: International Legitimacy
    • Issue: Assad’s regime remains internationally isolated, making it difficult to secure reconstruction funds or recognition.
    • Impact: Limits the government’s ability to stabilize and rebuild the country.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could offer security guarantees to attract Gulf states or Western support.

Kurds

  • Obstacle 1: Balancing Relations with the U.S. and Syrian Government
    • Issue: Cooperation with the U.S. alienates the Syrian government, while aligning with Assad risks losing U.S. protection and aid.
    • Impact: Limits autonomy negotiations and leaves the Kurds vulnerable to Turkish aggression.
    • Counterbalance: The Kurds could offer anti-terrorism cooperation to both the U.S. and Syria as leverage.
  • Obstacle 2: Dealing with Turkey
    • Issue: Kurdish ambitions for autonomy threaten Turkey’s national security interests.
    • Impact: Invites Turkish military incursions and reduces regional stability.
    • Counterbalance: The Kurds could agree to demilitarized zones near the Turkish border in exchange for security guarantees.
  • Obstacle 3: Lack of International Recognition
    • Issue: The Kurds lack formal recognition as a political entity, limiting their leverage in negotiations.
    • Impact: Makes it difficult to secure long-term autonomy or aid.
    • Counterbalance: Strengthening alliances with Western powers, particularly the U.S. and EU, for political support.

Russia

  • Obstacle 1: Maintaining Turkey-Russia Relations
    • Issue: Supporting Assad and Kurdish ambitions creates friction with Turkey, a key partner for energy exports.
    • Impact: Risks losing Turkey as a strategic ally and transit country for the TurkStream pipeline.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could mediate Turkish-Kurdish tensions to maintain balanced relations.
  • Obstacle 2: Balancing Iran and Israel
    • Issue: Russia’s partnership with Iran conflicts with its goal of stability in Syria, as Iran’s activities provoke Israeli airstrikes.
    • Impact: Undermines Russian efforts to stabilize Syria and risks alienating Israel.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could limit Iran’s military presence near Israeli borders to appease both Israel and the U.S.
  • Obstacle 3: U.S. Sanctions
    • Issue: Russia’s involvement in Syria contributes to continued U.S. sanctions, limiting economic recovery.
    • Impact: Weakens Russia’s ability to fund its military operations and aid Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could negotiate de-escalation agreements with the U.S. in exchange for reduced sanctions.

How Fado and Validation Are Connected:

  1. They know communication is imperfect
    • In Validation, people often misunderstand each other because they interpret words and actions through their own imago.
    • In Fado, the singer expresses deep emotions that words alone cannot fully communicate, and the music fills in those emotional gaps.
    • Both recognize that emotions are often felt rather than logically explained.
  2. They express deep emotions that words may fail to capture
    • Fado conveys saudade—a deep, untranslatable longing—through music, tone, and feeling, not just words.
    • Validation encourages people to express hurt, longing, and needs in a way the reciever can truly hear.
    • In both cases, emotions are not just stated—they are felt and received by the other person.
  3. They create a bridge between people who might not fully understand each other
    • In Validation, recievers truly listen and mirror the others' emotions and words, creating a sense of understanding and connection.
    • Fado helps listeners connect to the emotions of the singer, even if they don’t share the same experiences. The song’s sadness, longing, and hope become universal.
    • In both cases, the goal is to create emotional resonance—so that the listener doesn’t just "hear" the words but actually feels what the other person is feeling.
  4. They validate emotions through deep connection
    • In Validation, when a person’s emotions are truly heard and reflected back, they feel understood—which leads to accord.
    • In Fado, when someone listens and resonates with the song, they feel less alone in their emotions—as if the singer understands their pain.
    • The result in both cases is a sense of being seen, heard, and emotionally safe.
  5. They are somewhat universal. In other words, even if I do not agree with you, or have the same experience, I can empathize with you.

Two Cultural Perspectives on Time and the Future

  1. The Future is behind me. (Past-Oriented Perspective( This itself is a term that is culturally biased.))
    • The future is seen as the growing distance from past events, with time expanding forward.
    • Often found in cultures that emphasize historical continuity, tradition, and a strong connection to ancestors.
    • Example: Aymara speakers (South America) conceptualize the future as "behind" them and the past as "in front" because the past is known and visible, while the future is unknown and unseen.
  2. The future is ahead of me (Future-Oriented Perspective)
    • The future is viewed as approaching or compressing toward the present, often with a focus on deadlines and efficiency.
    • Common in Western, industrialized cultures that prioritize planning and goal-setting.
    • Example: English and Spanish speakers often say "The deadline is coming up" or "We are getting closer to the event," framing the future as something moving toward them.

  1. Intercultural Communication: The exchange of information between individuas from different backgrounds of learned behavior.

2. Culture: A series of behaviors that are invented, not acquired, and passed on through learning within a group.

3. Sender: The individual or entity that initiates a message in the communication process.

4. Receiver: The individual or entity that interprets and processes the message in the communication process.

5. Miscommunication: A failure to convey information accurately or understand a message as intended, often due to cultural differences or other factors.

6. Cultural Context: The background, habits, and perceptions shared by members of a group that influence how messages are sent and interpreted.

7. Verbal Communication: The exchange of information through spoken or written language.

8. Nonverbal Communication: The exchange of information through non-linguistic means, such as body language, facial expressions, or gestures.

9. Validation Steps: Setting an appointment, expressing appreciation, mirroring and summary, empathy, imago

10. Imago: In the context of psychology, particularly in Imago Therapy, it refers to an unconscious idealized (misguided) image of a person, often based on early childhood relationships, that influences adult relationships. Cultural imago is the misguided image of the world based upon traumatic history.

11. Validation: The act of recognizing or affirming the fact that a person’s thoughts, feelings, or experiences are “worthy” to be considered. It relates to neurological effects like reducing stress by lowering cortisol and adrenaline levels.

12. Filtering: The process of separating relevant information (meaning) from irrelevant information (noise) in communication.

13. Sojourner: An individual who temporarily resides in a different culture and must adapt to its communication norms and practices.

14. Noise: Anything that interferes with the transmission or understanding of a message. It could be literal background noise, but in this context, it more broadly includes any irrelevant information or distractions that could impede clear communication. Culture teaches us what is noise and what isn’t.

15. Regional cultures: Distinct groups that share common practices that develop within specific geographic regions, shaped by local traditions, customs, and social norms.

16. Mirror Neurons: Nerve cells in the brain  that fire both when an individual acts and when they observe the same action performed by another, playing a role in understanding others’ actions and intentions.

17. Cortisol: A hormone released by the adrenal glands in response to stress, playing a role in metabolism, immune response, and stress management.

18. Oxytocin: A hormone often associated with bonding, trust, and social connection, sometimes called the ‘love hormone.’

19. Adrenaline: A hormone released in response to stress, increasing heart rate, blood flow, and energy availability in the body, part of the ‘fight or flight’ response.

20. Mediation: A process where a neutral third party helps resolve a conflict or dispute by facilitating communication between the parties involved.

21. High-context Culture: A setting where much of the information is implied or understood through background knowledge, with a focus on non-verbal cues and shared assumption

22. Dopamine: A neurotransmitter involved in reward, motivation, and pleasure, playing a crucial role in the brain’s reward system.

New Vocabulary you can be tested on these words or the previous 22 on Wednesday.

23. Schema: the mental frameworks that individuals use to interpret and navigate social interactions, shaped by their cultural background, experiences, and expectations

24. Action-Perception Loop: the ongoing process where a person’s understanding of a situation shapes their response, and that response then affects how they interpret future interactions. Past experiences influence what they notice, which guides how they react, which guides what they notice, creating a cycle.

25. Assimilation: interpreting our new experiences in terms of our existing schemas.

26. Cultural Assimilation: The interpretation and adoption of elements of dominant collective customs and practices through the lens of a preexisting sense of self.

27. Accomodation: When new information challenges an existing schema, it is the process by which the individual must modify that schema or create a new schema.

28. Disequilibrium: A state of cognitive imbalance that occurs when new information does not fit into an existing schema. This can create confusion, uncertainty, or even resistance. (corisol and adrenaline responses)

29. Equilibration: The process of cognitive imbalance by either assimilating or accommodating the new information, restoring cognitive balance.

30. Priming: The activation of certain schemas in advance, influencing how new information is processed.

What does the 7-38-55% rule have to do with negotiation?

  • Observe your counterpart’s body language. According to the 7-38-55 rule, 93 percent of meaning is communicated non-verbally. Your tone of voice and body language are much more important than what you’re actually saying. If your counterpart’s body language indicates that they are about to lose their bearings, speak calmly and plainly to soothe them and slow the pace of the negotiation. You should always seek a course of action that encourages the other side to let their guard down. In an effective negotiation, you should try to build a working relationship with your negotiating partner and find ways to defuse tension when possible.
  • Look for inconsistencies between spoken words and nonverbal behavior. When you’re at the negotiating table, pay attention to how your counterparts speak and act. Do the words they’re saying match the way they’re carrying themselves? Look at the people who are not talking—what does their body language signal to you? Remember that their spoken words only account for seven percent of their communication and look for nonverbal cues that contradict their words. It’s also important that you make sure your own nonverbal messages are in line with what you are saying. If your facial expressions are pained and you can’t maintain eye contact, you are communicating your insecurity to your counterpart no matter what you say.
  • Monitor your counterpart’s speaking patterns. We all have one way of telling the truth. If you can identify how your counterpart looks and sounds when they are being honest with you, you’ll be able to detect any deviations from that pattern that may signal a lie. People who are being dishonest tend to use more words and effort than necessary to communicate their point. Use your listening skills to keep an ear out for such verbosity and gain an upper hand.
  • Learn to use different vocal tones. According to the 7-38-55 rule, tone of voice accounts for 38 percent of meaning in communication. Mastering the use of your voice can help you become a better negotiator by improving the delivery of your arguments. In the negotiating room, there are three main tones of voice: Assertive voice is declarative and typically counterproductive. An accommodating voice gently promotes collaboration and should be used most of the time.
  • Calibrate your own nonverbal communication. Effective communication during a negotiation, conflict management session, or problem-solving sessions requires the ability to calibrate how you communicate. Tap into your listening skills, assess how your counterpart is feeling, and adjust your nonverbal communication in response. This will communicate far more about your reaction than anything you could say to them. When debating the main points in a negotiation, try to alter your demeanor based on the signals you are receiving from your counterpart. Even if your arguments themselves don’t change, changing your nonverbal messaging can be effective.

What does the 7-38-55% rule have to do with negotiation?

  • Observe your counterpart’s body language. According to the 7-38-55 rule, 93 percent of meaning is communicated non-verbally. Your tone of voice and body language are much more important than what you’re actually saying. If your counterpart’s body language indicates that they are about to lose their bearings, speak calmly and plainly to soothe them and slow the pace of the negotiation. You should always seek a course of action that encourages the other side to let their guard down. In an effective negotiation, you should try to build a working relationship with your negotiating partner and find ways to defuse tension when possible.
  • Look for inconsistencies between spoken words and nonverbal behavior. When you’re at the negotiating table, pay attention to how your counterparts speak and act. Do the words they’re saying match the way they’re carrying themselves? Look at the people who are not talking—what does their body language signal to you? Remember that their spoken words only account for seven percent of their communication and look for nonverbal cues that contradict their words. It’s also important that you make sure your own nonverbal messages are in line with what you are saying. If your facial expressions are pained and you can’t maintain eye contact, you are communicating your insecurity to your counterpart no matter what you say.
  • Monitor your counterpart’s speaking patterns. We all have one way of telling the truth. If you can identify how your counterpart looks and sounds when they are being honest with you, you’ll be able to detect any deviations from that pattern that may signal a lie. People who are being dishonest tend to use more words and effort than necessary to communicate their point. Use your listening skills to keep an ear out for such verbosity and gain an upper hand.
  • Learn to use different vocal tones. According to the 7-38-55 rule, tone of voice accounts for 38 percent of meaning in communication. Mastering the use of your voice can help you become a better negotiator by improving the delivery of your arguments. In the negotiating room, there are three main tones of voice: Assertive voice is declarative and typically counterproductive. An accommodating voice gently promotes collaboration and should be used most of the time.
  • Calibrate your own nonverbal communication. Effective communication during a negotiation, conflict management session, or problem-solving sessions requires the ability to calibrate how you communicate. Tap into your listening skills, assess how your counterpart is feeling, and adjust your nonverbal communication in response. This will communicate far more about your reaction than anything you could say to them. When debating the main points in a negotiation, try to alter your demeanor based on the signals you are receiving from your counterpart. Even if your arguments themselves don’t change, changing your nonverbal messaging can be effective.

28. Disequilibrium: A state of cognitive imbalance that occurs when new information does not fit into an existing schema. This can create confusion, uncertainty, or even resistance. (corisol and adrenaline responses)

29. Equilibration: The process of cognitive imbalance by either assimilating or accommodating the new information, restoring cognitive balance.

30. Priming: The activation of certain schemas in advance, influencing how new information is processed

31. Collective individualism A cultural pattern where people prioritize group goals while maintaining personal autonomy (e.g., Japan).

32. Facework: The strategies that people use to maintain their own and others' social standing. (think "saving face"

33. Low-context culture: Practices and traditions in which communication is explicit and relies less on direct statements, and more on other cues.

34. Power Distance The extent to which a culture accepts and acknowledges differences in authority within hierarchical structures.

New Vocabulary for Wednesday>

  1. Centripetal Forces of Culture: These are circumstances that pull people toward a common center, creating unity and cohesion within a society.

2. Centrifugal Forces of Culture: These are circumstances that push people apart or away from the center, creating diversity and sometimes fragmentation.

3. Cultural imperative: a principle, value, belief, or practice that a society considers essential, non-negotiable, and fundamental to its identity and functioning.

4. The negotiation of cultural norms: a process within and between groups, involving collective actions that challenge, reinforce, and modify shared understandings of acceptable behaviors, values, and beliefs.

5. "Invented tradition": a set of practices, rituals, or symbols that are presented as being old and deeply rooted in the past, but which are, in fact, of relatively recent origin, often deliberately created

Declining PISA Scores Finland, once renowned for its high-achieving students, has experienced a steady decline in its PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment) scores since 2007, coinciding with the introduction of smartphones1. The latest PISA study revealed Finland's lowest-ever average scores in math, science, and reading, prompting the Finnish Ministry of Education and Culture to describe the situation as "extremely disconcerting"1. Digital Distraction The 2022 PISA data showed that over 80% of Finland's 15-year-olds reported being distracted by digital devices during math class, at least sometimes1. This high level of distraction is strongly associated with lower academic achievement. Excessive Screen Time Finnish teenagers reported spending more than four hours on digital devices during the school day, ranking Finland sixth overall in digital device usage at school according to the 2022 PISA study1. This excessive screen time is likely contributing to the erosion of learning outcomes. Early Smartphone Adoption A particularly concerning trend in Finland is the early age at which children receive smartphones: Most Finnish children receive their first smartphone (or smartwatch) at age 5 or 61. A 2022 survey indicated that virtually all first-graders in Finland owned phones, including phone watches1. This early adoption of smartphones may be exacerbating the "phone-based childhood" phenomenon, which has been linked to sleep loss, addiction, attention problems, and social deprivation1.
